query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: High-chromium steels resist corrosion in chemically aggressive and nuclear-power environments by rapidly forming a continuous, protective chromium oxide (Cr2O3) film. This film acts as a diffusion barrier that limits oxygen and corrosive species ingress, thereby reducing the overall corrosion rate compared to low-chromium steels.
generation.material_initial_state: Polished steel samples with controlled microstructure; one set with high chromium content and one set with low chromium content.
generation.intervention: Expose paired high- and low-chromium steel samples to simulated corrosive environments, such as high-temperature aqueous media with controlled pH and halide concentrations.
generation.conditions: Test conditions reflecting chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications: elevated temperature, defined pH and chloride (or other halide) concentration, and controlled oxygen content; exposure durations sufficient to allow the formation and stabilization of oxide layers.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, thin, Cr-rich passivation layer (primarily chromium oxide, Cr2O3) that forms on the surface of high-chromium steels.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of chromium in the alloy leads to the rapid formation of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 layer. This layer provides a physical and chemical barrier that impedes further oxidation and metal dissolution, while low-chromium steels form less protective or discontinuous oxides that fail to prevent corrosion effectively.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical exposure, high-chromium steels will develop a more uniform and less permeable Cr2O3 layer, resulting in a significantly reduced corrosion rate relative to low-chromium steels. Baseline observations in the low-chromium samples should show thicker, discontinuous, or mixed oxide films with higher rates of metal loss.
generation.baseline: Corrosion behavior and oxide film characteristics of low-chromium steels under the same simulated environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in environments that mimic the temperature, chemical (pH, halides), and oxidative conditions typical of chemical processing and nuclear-power systems. It may not apply in environments where alternative corrosion mechanisms (e.g., molten salt corrosion or extreme mechanical erosion) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxide formation and its long-term stability might be affected by additional factors such as microstructural variations and minor alloying species. The extent and uniformity of the protective Cr2O3 film across different steel grades are also subject to experimental variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare matched sets of high-chromium and low-chromium steel samples with identical microstructural histories. Expose these samples to a controlled high-temperature aqueous environment with fixed pH and halide concentration. Periodically extract samples to perform surface analysis and corrosion rate measurements.
measurements: Surface composition and oxide layer continuity using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS)
Morphological analysis via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Quantitative corrosion rate measurements by weight loss or electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-chromium steel samples do not form a more continuous, Cr-rich oxide layer than the low-chromium samples, or if their corrosion rate is not significantly lower under the same conditions, then the hypothesis that the protective Cr2O3 film is the primary mechanism of corrosion resistance is falsified.

With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed.
